Haiggulim lazzaggim. iggul kemin rechayim gadol hayu mesimin al hazzagim leachar sheddarchu haanavim baregel, kede sheyyitmatztzu veyetze kol hayyayin hannishar bahen, umittoch kavdo vegadlo shel iggul ze tzerichim bene adam harebe lehaaloto al hatztzibbur shel hazzagin heasuy kemin tappuach ulehorido, lechach necheshav reshut harabbim letaher sefek tuma, mishshum derabbim metzuyin sham:
Kerem shellifne habbotzrim reshut hayyachid. sheyyerein bene adam likkanes sham, mippene shennitpas alav kegannav:
Achar habbotzrim reshut harabbim. sheyyesh reshut lechol adam likkanes:
Kele vet habbad shel gat. kelomar veshel gat. devet habbad leshemen, vegat leyayin:
Haekel. asuy kemin kuppa mesoreget keen reshet, veachar shessachatu hazzetim notnim haggefet beoto ekel, umannichim alav davar machbid lehotzi hannishar:
Menaggevan. vekodem lachen lo mehaneya tevila im nitmeu, ad sheyyetze mehen hammashke hattame shennidbak bahen:
Choltan. shofech alehen mayim rotchim veachar kach matbilan:
Beshibbolet hannahar. makom shehammayim rodfin, kede lehotzi hammashke hannidbak bahen. veen halacha kerabbi yose:
Nimtza al gabbe ferudim. leachar shettaka yated baom lehaferid haom lechamma chalakim perudim, uvechol gush vegush meelle hachalakim happerudim mehaom yesh zetim medubbakim:
Vehu nogea bechabbetza. sheim bata letzaref zetim shehashsheretz nogea bahen yesh bahen kabbetza:

Tame. kol haggush. af al gav deen haggush chibbur mishshettaka et hayyated baom lehaferidam, mikkol makom kevan deyesh begush ze zetim temein keshiur letamme acherim, dehaynu kabbetza, naasa chibbur letamme kol shear hazzetim shebbo:
Perudim al gabbe ferudim. sheyyesh gushim al gabbe gushim vehashsheretz al haggush haelyon:
Af al pi shehashsheretz nogea bechabbetza. shel oto gush:
En tame ella mekom maggao. shel sheretz, kelomar oto gush bilvad shehashsheretz naga bo. aval shear gushim, tehorim:
Nimtza. hashsheretz:
Ben hakkotel lazzetim tahor. velo chayshinan shemma haya al hazzetim:
Nimtza vaggag. hammaale zetim min hammaatan laggag, venimtza sheretz achar kach bazzetim sheal haggag:
Hammaatan tahor. kelomar zetim shebbammaatan tehorin, velo amrinan im hazzetim huva vehaya bammaatan:
Nimtza vammaatan. zetim sheheela baggag, temein, demikkodem sheheela hazzetim laggag haya hashsheretz bammaatan:
Nimtza saruf. vesheretz saruf lo metamme, dichtiv [vayyikra 11] bemotam, keen motam. ucheshennimtza saruf al gabbe zetim tehorim, lo chayshinan shemma naga bahen kodem shennisraf:
Mehuha. beged shennitcharech baesh venaasa kemin kure akkavish, veshuv eno mekabbel tuma:
Tehora. velo amrinan shemma tame haya mittechilla kodem shennitcharech:
Kishat metziatan. ben lehakel ben lehachemir:
Kevan shehishshikah lammikve. kevan shechibber katze echad min hammakkel bammikve, af al pi shello hitbilo kullo, taharu kol hammashkin temein shebberosho haacher, diktafres chibbur:
Ad sheyyatbil et kullah. dekasavre rabbanan ketafres eno chibbur:
Hannitztzok. killuach tzinnor habba millemala lematta bizkifa keammud:
Ketafres. mayim habbaim millemala lematta derech midron shel tel gavoah:
Umashke tofeach. veen bo tofeach al menat lehatepiach, sheen bo kol kach mashke sheim tafach bahen yado ala bah mashke sheyyuchal lehatepiach davar acher:

Eno chibbur lo lattuma. sheim mashkim telushin hen venaga tame battachton, haelyon tahor. vechen leinyan mashke tofeach, vaafillu bemakom chalak, im mashkin mikkan umashkin mikkan umashke tofeach beemtza, naga tame bemashke tofeach, mashkin shemmikkan umikkan tehorim af al pi shemmechubbarim lo:
Velo lattohora. kegon gumma sheen bah arbaim sea, venitztzok o mashke tofeach mechubbar legumma zo ulemikve kasher, eno chibbur, vehattovel begumma zo lo alta lo tevila:
Eshboren. makom amok shennikvu bo mayim:
Chibbur lattuma velattohora. veim nitmeu ketzatan nitmeu kullan. vechen im nitchabberu ketzat mehen lammikve vetaharu, taharu kullan:
Mishsheyare. mishshiyyure. shelleachar shemmetu kullan nishtayyera hakkabbala beyado. vehu haya kohen gadol achar ezra:
Hu haya omer. kelomar kach haya meraggela befumeh tamid. vechen kol rabbi peloni omer, hu haya omer, shebbemassechta zo, perushan haya ragil lomar ken tamid:
Haolam omed. lo nivra haolam ella bishvil shelosha devarim hallalu:
Al hattora. sheilmale lo kibbelu yisrael et hattora lo nivreu shamayim vaaretz, dichtiv (yirmeya log) im lo veriti yomam valayla chukkot shamayim vaaretz lo samti (shabbat pach.):

Veal haavoda. avodat hakkarbanot. shekkach shaninu bemassechet taanit (27:), sheilmale maamadot lo nitkayyemu shamayim vaaretz. umatzinu shebbishvil hakkarbanot shehikriv noach nishba [hakkadosh baruch hu] shello yavi mabbul laolam. hare shehaolam omed al hakkarbanot:
Veal gemilut chasadim. dichtiv (tehillim 89) olam chesed yibbane. ugemilut chasadim, hu lesammeach chatanim, ulenachem avelim, ulevakker cholim, velikbor metim, vechayyotze vaze:
Hazzolef et habbor. hammotzi yayin veshemen shebbabbor. umippene sheeno motzio kullo bevat achat ella meat meat, kare leh zolef:
Venimtza sheretz barishona. shehichnis chavit babbor umilleah, vechen sheniyya, vechen shelishit, veachar kach nimtza sheretz bechavit shemmille rishona:
Kullan temeot. demeharishona nitma kol ma shebbabbor, ben shehaya sheretz babbor ben shehaya bechavit:
Baacharona hi temea vechullan tehorot. demimmenna haya hashsheretz velo min habbor. vaafillu haya min habbor, shemma nafal babbor achar shennitmalleu kol harishonot:
Ematay bizman shehu zolef. keshehu machnis hechaviyyot atzman betoch habbor umemalle otan achat achat:
Aval haya zolef bemachatz. shehechaviyyot omdot chutz labbor, vehu memalle otan al yede hammachatz, vehu keli cheres heasuy lemalleot bo yayin:
Nimtza sheretz beachat mehen hi temea bilvad. deemur betoch hechavit haya hashsheretz velo babbor:

Ematay bizman shehu vodek. hammachatz vehechaviyyot. shebbedakan shello haya bahen sheretz kodem shennatan letocho shemen, aval lo haya mechasse lo habbor velo hechaviyyot kol shaa shehaya mevi hammachatz mizze laze, deemur bahalichato nafal hashsheretz bechavit. vechen mechasse velo bodek nammi shemma haya bechavit kodem lachen:

Aval haya vodek umechasse. shebbadak hechaviyyot, uvechol paam shehaya molich hammachatz mizze laze haya mechasse ben bor ben chavit, mimma nafshach sheretz haya babbor mittechillato, ben shennimtza bechavit, ben shennimtza babbor, ben shennimtza bammachatz:

rashi: Vayyikchu et kol hashalal vegomer'. maggid shehayu chesherim vetzaddikim, velo nechshedu al haggezzel lishloach yad babbizza shello virshut, shenneemar et kol hashalal vegomer', vaalehem meforash bakkabbala "shinnayich keeder harechelim" vego' (Shir Hashirim 6:6) — af anshe hammilchama shebbach kullam tzaddikim:
Shalal. hen mittaltelin shel malbush vetachshitin:
Baz. hu vizzat mittaltelin sheenam tachshit:
Malakoch. adam uvehema, uvemakom shekkatuv shevi etzel malkoach, shevi vaadam umalkoach babbehema:
Vayyetzeu moshe veelazar hakkohen. lefi sherau et naare yisrael yotzeim lachatof min habbizza (sifre):
Vayyiktzof moshe al pekude hechayil. memunnim al hachayil, lelammedcha shekkol sirchon haddor taluy baggedolim sheyyesh koach beyadam limchot (sham):
Michutz lammachane. shello yikkanesu laazara:

Kol horeg nefesh. ra' meir omer behoreg bedavar hamkabbel tuma hakkatuv medabber, velimmedcha hakkatuv shehakkeli metamme adam bechibbure hammet keillu nogea bammet atzmo, o yachol afillu zarak bo chetz vaharago? talmud lomar vakal naga bachalal, hikkish horeg lenogea, ma nogea al yede chibburo, af horeg aye chibburo (Sifre Bamidbar 19):

Titchatteu. beme nidda kedin shear temee metim, sheaf ledivre haomerim kivre goyim enam metammein baohel, shenneemar (Yechezkel 34) "veatten tzoni tzon mariti adam attem" — attem keruyim adam — mode hu shehaggoyim metammeim bemagga uvemassa, shello neemar adam ella etzel tumat oholot, shenneemar "adam ki yamut beohel" (Bamidbar 19):
Attem ushevichem. lo shehaggoyim mekabbelin tuma utzerichin hazzaa, ella ma attem bene verit, af shevichem kesheyyavou labberit veyittameu, tzerichin hazzaa (sifre):
Vechol maase izzim. lehavi chele hakkarnayim vehattelafayim vehaatzamot (Chullin 25):

Vayyomer elazar hakkohen vegomer'. lefi shebba moshe lichlal kaas ba lichlal taut, shennitallemu mimmennu hilchot giule goyim, vechen atta motze vashemini lammilluim, shenneemar "vayyiktzof al elazar veal itamar" (Vayikra 10) — ba lichlal kaas ba lichlal taut, vechen beshimu na hammorim (Bamidbar 20) "vayyach et hassela" — al yede hakkaas taa (Sifre; Fesachim 66):
Asher tzivva Adonai vegomer'. tala hahoraa berabbo (80' Sifre):

Ach et hazzahav vegomer'. aapi shello hizhir lachem moshe ella al hilchot tuma, od yesh lehazhir lachem al hilchot giul, veach" leshon miut, kelomar memuatin attem millehishtammesh bakkelim afillu leachar taharatan mittumat hammet ad sheyyitharu mibbeliat issur nevelot; verabbotenu ameru, ak et hazahab lomar, shetztzarich lehaavir chaluda shello kodem sheyyagilennu, vezehu leshon ak, shello yehe sham chaluda ach hammattechet yihye kemo shehu:
Kol davar asher yavo vaesh. levashel bo kelum:
Taaviru vaesh. kederech tashmisho hagalato — mi shettashmisho al yede chammin yagilennu vechammin, umi shettashmisho aye tzeli, kegon hashefud vehaaskela, yelabbeno baur (Avoda Zara 74):

Ach beme nidda yitchatta. lefi feshuto chittuy ze letaharo mittumat met, amar lahem tzerichin hakkelim giul letaharam min haissur vechittuy letaharan min hattuma; verabbotenu dareshu mikkan sheaf lehachshiran min haissur hitin tevila lichle mattachot, ume nidda hakketuvin kan dareshu mayim hareuyim litbol bahem nidda, vechamma hem? arbaim sea (Sham 75):
Vechol asher lo yavo vaesh. kol davar sheen tashmisho al yede haur, kegon kosot utzelochiyyot shettashmishan betzonen velo valeu issur:
Taaviru vammayim. matbilan vedayyo, vedavka chele mattachot:
El hammachane. lemachane shechina, sheen teme met taun shilluach mimmachane leviyya umimmachane yisrael:
Sa et rosh. kach et hacheshbon:
Vechatzita et hammalkoach ben tofese hammilchama vegomer'. chetzyo laellu vechetzyo laellu:
Bevet aviha. birshut aviha vaafillu enah beveto (sham):

Binureha. velo ketanna velo vogeret, shehakketanna en nidrah neder, vehabbogeret enah birshuto shel aviha lehafer nedareha; vee zo hi ketanna? ameru rabbotenu bat 11 shana veyom echad nedareha nivdakin, im yoda leshem mi nodra uleshem mi hikdisha, nidrah neder, bat 12 shana veyom echad enah tzericha libbadek:

Veim heni aviha otah. im mana otah min hanneder, kelomar shehefer lah. hanaa zo eni yodea ma hi, keshehu omer "veim beyom shemoa ishah yani otah vehefer" (Pasuk 9) heve omer hanaa zo hafara. ufeshuto leshon menia vahasara, vechen "velamma teniun" (Bamidbar 32), vechen "shemen rosh al yani roshi" (tehillim kma), vechen "vidatem et tenuati" (Bamidbar 14) — et asher sartem mealay:

Vaadonai' yislach lah. bamme hakkatuv medabber? beisha shennodra venazir veshama balah vehefer lah vehi lo yoda veoveret al nidrah veshota yayin umittammea lemetim, zo hi shetztzericha selicha veaapi shehu mufar, veim hammufarin tzerichim selicha, kava lesheenan mufarim (80' Kiddushin 81):

Veim hayo tihye leish. zo arusa, o eno ella nesua? keshehu omer "veim bet ishah nadara" hare nesua amur, vechan baarusa, uva lachalok bah sheaviha uvalah meferin nedareha, hefer haav velo hefer habbaal, o hefer habbaal velo hefer haav, hare ze eno mufar, veen tzarich lomar im kiyyem echad mehem:
Unedareha aleha. shennodra bevet aviha, velo shama bahen aviha velo huferu velo hukemu (80' Sifre):
Veshama ishah vegomer'. hare lecha sheim kiyyem habbaal shehu kayyam:
Vehefer et nidrah. yachol afillu lo hefer haav, tal (Pasuk 17) "binureha bet aviha" — kol shebbinureha birshut aviha hi (sifre sham):

Kol asher osra al nafshah yakum aleha. lefi sheenah lo virshut av velo virshut baal, uvealmana min hannissuin hakkatuv medabber, aval almana min haerusin — met habbaal nitrokena vechozra reshut laav (Nedarim 70):
Veim bet ashah nadara. binsua hakkatuv medabber (Sham 67):

Kol neder vechol shevuat issar vegomer'. lefi sheamar shehabbaal mefer, yachol kol nedarim vemashma, tal lanat napash — eno mefer ella nidre innuy nefesh bilvad, vehem meforashim bemasse' nedarim (Daf 79):
Miyyom el yom. shello tomar meet leet, lechach neemar "miyyom el yom", lelammedcha sheen mefer ella ad shettechshach (Nedarim 76):
Lechol mattot yisrael. lerabbot shevet levi (sifre):

Vayyimmaseru. lehodiacha shivchan shel roe yisrael kamma hem chavivim al yisrael, ad shello shameu vemitato ma hu omer? "od meat usekaluni" (Shemot 17), umisheshameu shemmitat moshe teluya venikmat midyan lo ratzu lalechet ad shennimseru al korchan (sifre):

targum: Vahava techumehon mimachanayim kol matnan kol malchuteh deog malka dematnan vechol kafrane yair divmatnan shittin kirvin:
Ufalgut ara degilad veashtarot veedrei kirvaya malchuteh deog bematnan livne machir bar menashe lefalgut bene machir lezarayathon:
Ilen di achasin moshe bemesheraya demoav meivera leyardena diricho madinecha:
Uleshivta delevi la yehav moshe achasana mattenan dihav lehon Adonai elaha deyisrael inun achasantehon kema demalel lehon:

rashi: Tirotam. mekom notirin shellahem, shehu leshon moshav kumarim yodee chukkehem; daa — leshon moshav sarehem, kemo shemmeturgam "sarne felishtim" (Shmuel 1 6) — turene felishtae:
Umimmachatzit bene yisrael asher chatza moshe. laeda, vehotziah lahem man hanashim hatzabaim:
Vattehi mechetzat haeda. kach vechach:
Vayyikkach moshe vegomer'.
Happekudim. hamemunnim:
Etzada. ellu tzemidim shel regel:
Vetzamid. shel yad:
Agil. nizme ozen:
Vechumaz. defus shel bet harechem, lechapper hirhur hallev shel benot midyan (Shabbat 64):
Mikkadesh barnea. kach shemah, ushette kadesh hayu:
Hakkenizzi. chorego shel kenaz haya veyolda lo immo shel kalev et otniel (Sota 11):
Vayniem. vaytaltelem, min "na vanad" (Bereshit 4):
Lispot. kemo "sefu shana al shana" (Yeshayahu 29), "olotechem sefu" vego' (Yirmeyahu 7), leshon tosefet:
Vaytzav lahem. kemo alehem, veal tenaam minna elazar vihoshua, kemo "Adonai yillachem lachem" (Shemot 14):
Veittanu achuzzat nachalatenu. kelomar beyadenu uvirshutenu tehi achuzzat nachalatenu meever hazze:
Are mivtzar vegidrot tzon. ze sof pasuk musav al techillat hainyan — vayyivnu vene gad et hearim hallalu lihyot are mivtzar vegidrot tzon:

Veet nevo veet baal meon musabbot shem. nevo uvaal meon shemot aza hem, vehayu haemoriyyim korim arehem al shem aza shellahem, uvene reuven hesebbu et shemam leshemot acherim, vezehu mosabat sham — nevo uvaal meon musabbot leshem acher:
Veet sivma. banu sivma, vehi sevam haamura lemala:
Vayyoresh. ketargumo "vetarich", shettevat resh meshammeshet shette machalakot, leshon yerusha uleshon horasha shehu terud veteruch:
Chavvotehem. kafranehon:
Vayyikra ethen chavvot yair. lefi shello hayu lo vanim keraatam bishmo lezikkaron:

Vayyikra la novach. "la" eno mappik hea, veraiti visodo shel ra' moshe haddarshan lefi shello nitkayyem lah shem ze lefichach hu rafe, shemmashmaut midrasho kemo lo; utemehani ma yidrosh bishte tevot haddomot lah "vayyomer la voaz" (Rut 2), "livnot la vayit" (Zecharya 5):

Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 13:68-: And after we have spoken of the parts of slander as found in the books, we must explain the punishment of one who accepts the evil report. In Tractate Pesachim (118a), Rav Sheshet said in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, whoever speaks slander, whoever accepts slander, and whoever testifies falsely against his fellow, deserves to be cast to the dogs, as it is said (Exodus 22:30), "you shall cast it to the dogs," and right after it, "you shall not accept a false report" - to this point. And in the Mechilta they said, "keep far from a false matter" (Exodus 23:7) - this is a warning to those who accept slander.

Further, they said in Pesachim (87b), why did Jeroboam merit to be counted among the kings of Israel and Judah? Because he did not accept slander, and so on - see there. And we also find that because David accepted slander from Ziba concerning Mephibosheth, the kingdom of the house of David was divided, as we read in Tractate Shabbat (56b): they said, of blessed memory, Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, at the time David said to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 19:30), "you and Ziba shall divide the field," a heavenly voice went out and said, Rehoboam and Jeroboam shall divide the kingdom. And if in a matter of recognizable facts, [David's error in] considering the matter believable caused such a great breach through the acceptance of slander, all the more so must a person distance himself and stop his ears from hearing the slander spoken every day about innocent people.

And one who accepts slander and shows in his soul that he agrees with the speaker and believes the words in front of people, is as though he spoke it, for he assists in the evil and causes disgrace to his fellow - for when the informer sees the face of the listener frowning, he ceases his words, but if he sees that the listener heeds him, he will not withhold his lies. And to this we were warned, "you shall not accept a false report" - that we not believe in our hearts a slanderous report, holding in our thoughts that those words are true, to disgrace the one about whom they are said, Heaven forfend.

And in Tanna DeVei Eliyahu (Zuta, chapter 7), they said, of blessed memory: it is said of Jeroboam ben Yoash that he showed honor to prophets - and what the Holy One, blessed be He, did not give into the hand of Joshua son of Nun and into the hand of David king of Israel, He gave into his hand, as it is said (2 Kings 14:25), "he restored the border of Israel from the entrance of Hamath to the sea of the Arabah." Similarly you say (2 Kings 14:26), "for the LORD saw the affliction of Israel, that it was very bitter, for there was none shut up or left at large, nor any helper for Israel; and the LORD had not said He would blot out the name of Israel from under heaven" - and what merit did Jeroboam have in this matter, was he not an idol worshipper? Rather, it was because he did not accept slander against the prophet Amos, as it is said (Amos 7:10), "then Amaziah the priest of Bethel sent to Jeroboam king of Israel, saying, Amos has conspired against you," and so on, "thus says Amos, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be exiled from its land" - he immediately rebuked him and expelled him with a reproof, saying, Heaven forfend, that righteous man did not prophesy this prophecy of his own accord, but from Heaven. At that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, said, a generation that worships idols, the head of the generation worships idols, yet did not accept slander - the land that I promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, to your seed I shall give it, I shall give into his hand, and he restored the border of Israel - to this point.

And further, among the things that blemish the covenant of the tongue, related to the matter of slander, is that one must be careful not to curse his fellow by the Name - even without mentioning the LORD, only in a foreign language, it is forbidden and transgresses a negative commandment - and even bringing forth a curse from his mouth unintentionally is unfitting, for a covenant is made with the lips (Mo'ed Katan 18a), and how many have been punished for this, as it is said in the Talmud several times (ibid.), "it was like an error that goes out from before a ruler."

And he says in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach, page 175a), concerning the death of Rachel, that our father Jacob, peace be upon him, caused her death by cursing without intent, in these words: Rabbi Yosi said, it is written (Proverbs 26:2), "a causeless curse shall not [lo] come" - and they established it as "lo" with a vav [meaning "to him," implying it does come, but to the curser]. And if it is a righteous person's curse, even if he did not intend it, once it emerges from his mouth, that evil inclination takes it and accuses with it at a time of danger. Jacob said (Genesis 31:32), "with whomever you find your gods, he shall not live" - and although he did not know, that Satan, who is always found among people, took that word. And therefore we have learned, a person should never open his mouth to Satan, because he takes that word and accuses with it above and below - all the more so a word of a sage or a word of a righteous person - to this point.

And so they said, of blessed memory, in Tractate Makkot (11a): Rabbi Abahu said, the curse of a sage, even if for no reason, comes to pass - from where do we know this? From Eli, who said to Samuel (1 Samuel 3:17), "so may God do to you, and more also, if you hide a word from me" - and although it is written, "and Samuel told him all the words and hid nothing from him," it is written (ibid. 8:3), "and his sons did not walk in his ways." And they brought another proof there, which we shall not copy, so as not to be lengthy.

And of this kind is that one should not curse someone who does not hear him, as the Targum explains on (Exodus 19:14, actually Leviticus 19:14) "you shall not curse the deaf" - do not curse one who does not hear. And so they said in the Zohar (Parashat Kedoshim, page 85a): come and see, whoever curses his fellow while he is present and shames him is as though he shed his blood, and this has been established. But this verse speaks of one who curses someone not with him, and that word curses him - and there is no single word that emerges from his mouth that has no voice, and that voice ascends above, and how many recorders join with that voice, until it ascends and arouses the place of the great abyss, as they have established, and how many are aroused against that person - woe to whoever brings forth an evil word from his mouth, and this has been established - to this point. And the pious author of Chovot HaLevavot wrote (Gate of Love of God, chapter 6), how despicable are the common people in this, bringing forth curses and blasphemies from their mouths.

Further, one should be careful not to curse himself in anger - for in the fourth palace of the palaces of the husks there are powers called "cursers of the day," who take that curse a person cursed himself with and fulfill it, Heaven forfend (Parashat Pekudei, page 266a). And this is one of the three things that cause harm to oneself, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Bereshit, page 14b, and also page 8b), that because David said (2 Samuel 12:5), "the man who did this deserves death," and so on, Dumah seized him, and had the Holy One, blessed be He, not assisted him, he would have fallen into the hand of Dumah, as King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 94:17), "unless the LORD had been my help, my soul would have soon dwelt in Dumah [silence/the netherworld]."

And concerning something similar, they said, of blessed memory, that a person should never open his mouth to Satan, as we read in the chapter "Mi SheMeto" (Berachot 19a), in these words: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, and so it was taught in the name of Rabbi Yosi, a person should never open his mouth to Satan. And Rav Yosef said, what is the verse? As it is said (Isaiah 1:9), "we would have been almost like Sodom" - what did the prophet answer him? (ibid. 1:10), "hear the word of the LORD, you rulers of Sodom." And it says further there, before this, that for this reason the mourner should not say, in acknowledging divine judgment, "Master of the universe, I have sinned much before You and You have not exacted from me one part in a thousand." And likewise it is fitting that a man not curse his wife, for the male is half the body, and the two of them together are one complete person - and if he curses her he is found cursing himself.

And it appears to me that the warning for all these aspects is from the verse (Exodus 23:13), "and make no mention of the name of other gods" - for all the blemishes of the tongue are from the side of the external force, which is "other gods." And so King David, peace be upon him, said (Psalms 34:14), "guard your tongue from evil" - the intent being that all things that have a grasp on "ra" [evil], which is Samael - and when he guards his tongue, he shall merit life and good, as it says (Psalms 34:13), "who is the man who desires life, who loves days," and so on.
And with this the chapter is concluded:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:1-1: After we have spoken, in the previous chapters, of the matter of the four groups that do not receive the countenance of the Shechinah, it remains for us to explain, in this chapter, the matter of vows and oaths that depend on the tongue, and likewise all the other things that blemish speech.

Concerning the matter of oaths, Rabbi Yitzchak Aboab, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer Menorat HaMaor (part 1, letter 38), in these words: those who swear by the blessed Name mean to say that just as He, blessed be He, is true, so their words are true, whether past or future - and one who swears falsely is like one who denies the truth of the Name. And if a person swears by the head of a king of flesh and blood and does not fulfill his word, he is deserving of death, since he has disgraced the king's honor - and if this is fitting to do to one who swears by a king of flesh and blood, who comes from a putrid drop and shall eventually die, all the more so must a person guard his mouth and tongue lest it cause him to make his flesh sin by swearing falsely by the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, who lives and endures forever. And we already know what happened to the children of Israel because they swore publicly concerning the matter of the concubine at Gibeah, and likewise the famine the Name brought upon the land because of Saul and his house, who transgressed the oath of the princes who swore to the Gibeonites (Bamidbar Rabbah 5:3). And we see that no explicit punishment is written in the warnings of the Ten Commandments except for idolatry and "you shall not take [the Name in vain]" - and yet people are so accustomed to this matter that some transgress it a hundred times a day without receiving any benefit.

And because people are not expert in the severity of an oath and its great weight, they come to blind their eyes and swear falsely - therefore our Rabbis instituted that the court, in every era, inform the one taking the oath of the severity of the oath and its law, in language he understands, in order to open his ear, so that perhaps he fear and withdraw from the oath - as we read in Tractate Shevuot (38b): our Rabbis taught, the oath of judges is also stated in its own language - they say to him, know that the whole world trembled at the time the Holy One, blessed be He, said (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain" - and for all the transgressions in the Torah, punishment is exacted from him alone, but here, from him and from his family, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" - and "his flesh" refers only to his relative, as it is said (Isaiah 58:7), "and do not hide yourself from your own flesh." And for all the transgressions in the Torah, punishment is exacted from him alone, but here, from him and from the whole world, as it is said (Hosea 4:2), "swearing falsely," and it is written (ibid. 4:3), "therefore the land mourns." And for all the transgressions in the Torah, if he has merit, they suspend [punishment] for two or three generations, but here punishment is exacted immediately, as it is said (Zechariah 5:4), "I have sent it forth, says the LORD, and it shall enter the house of the thief" - "I have sent it forth" - immediately; "and it shall enter the house of the thief" - this is one who steals his fellow's mind, that he has no claim against him, yet sues him and makes him swear; "and into the house of him who swears falsely by My Name" - literally; "and it shall lodge inside his house, and shall consume it, with its timber and its stones," and so on - from here you learn of things that fire and water do not destroy, but a false oath destroys them.

And further, we find that the sin of a false oath is equated with the desecration of the Name, as it is said (Avot, chapter 5, mishnah 9), "wild beasts come into the world because of a false oath and because of the desecration of the Name." And further we read in the Sifrei (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear falsely by My Name" - what does this teach? Since it is said (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain," one might think one is liable only concerning the Explicit Name alone - from where do we include all the appellations? Scripture says "by My Name" - any name that is Mine. "And you shall profane the Name" - this teaches that a false oath is a desecration of the Name. And we read in Midrash Tanchuma, whoever betrays through oaths denies the Holy One, blessed be He, and has no forgiveness ever, as it is said (Exodus 20:7), "for [the LORD] will not hold guiltless" - to this point. And I have condensed his words to what is necessary for our purpose, so as not to be lengthy.

Further, we read in Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot), in these words, on (Numbers 30:3), "if a man vows a vow to the LORD" - this is what is written (Jeremiah 4:2), "and you shall swear, as the LORD lives, in truth, in judgment, and in righteousness" - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to Israel, do not suppose that you are permitted to swear by My Name - even in truth you are not permitted to swear by My Name, unless all these qualities are in you: "you shall fear the LORD your God" - that you be like those called God-fearing, Abraham, Job, and Joseph - Abraham, as it is written (Genesis 22:12), "for now I know that you fear God"; Job, as it is written (Job 1:1), "a blameless and upright man, who feared God"; Joseph, as it is written (Genesis 42:18), "I fear God" - this is "you shall fear the LORD your God." "And Him shall you serve" - if you turn yourself to Torah and to occupy yourself with commandments and have no other service - therefore it says "and Him shall you serve." "And to Him shall you cleave" - but can a person cleave to the Shechinah? Has it not already been said (Deuteronomy 4:24), "for the LORD your God is a consuming fire"? Rather, this teaches you: whoever gives his daughter in marriage to a Torah scholar who reads and studies, does business for him, and benefits him from his possessions - concerning him it is said "and to Him shall you cleave." If you have all these qualities, you are permitted to swear, and if not, you are not permitted to swear. There was a story of King Yannai, who had two thousand towns, all of which were destroyed because of true oaths - how so? A person would say to his fellow, by an oath, I am going and shall eat such-and-such in such-and-such a place, and drink such-and-such in such-and-such a place, and they would go and fulfill their oaths, and [the towns] were destroyed - and if one who swears truly [causes such destruction], all the more so one who swears falsely - to this point.

And on the verse "you shall not take" (Exodus 20:7), they explained in the Mechilta, in these words: "you shall not take" - why is this said? Because it says (Leviticus 19:12), "and you shall not swear falsely by My Name" - I know only that one should not swear falsely; from where do we know he should not accept upon himself to swear [falsely, i.e., accept a false oath from another]? Scripture says (Exodus 20:7), "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God" - before you accept upon yourself to swear, I am your God; once you accept upon yourself to swear [falsely], I am your Judge - as it is said, "for the LORD will not hold guiltless one who takes His Name in vain." It is impossible to say "will not hold guiltless," since it is already said (ibid. 34:7), "and He will hold guiltless" [in some readings]; and it is impossible to say "will hold guiltless," since it is already said "will not hold guiltless" - say from now: He holds guiltless those who repent, and does not hold guiltless those who do not repent - to this point, their wording.

And by the plain meaning, "you shall not take" [lo tissa] is explained as meaning that a person should not accustom himself to bring up [lasat] the Name of Heaven with his mouth in vain, along the lines of (Psalms 16:4), "nor will I take up their names upon my lips" - and so Ramban, peace be upon him, explained.

And in the Tikkunim (page 118a), concerning the severity of the sin of oaths, they said, in these words: but others, from whose mouths emerge breaths of an [false] oath, of them it is said (Proverbs 7:26), "for she has cast down many wounded" - and these are called "wounded," for they desecrate the Name of the LORD, and breaths emerge from their mouths - and likewise those whose speech is falsehood and swearing falsely, and mention His Name in vain and falsely - with that Name that emerges for vanity and falsehood, they build buildings that nullify them from the world - this is what is written (Jeremiah 2:30), "in vain have I struck your children" - woe to those people from whose mouths emerge false words and oaths - it were better for them not to have come into the world. All the colleagues rose and said, may the Merciful One save us, may the Merciful One save us - to this point, their wording. Also in the Zohar (Parashat Yitro, pages 87b, 91b), in explaining the verse, they elaborate on the severity of the sin, and we shall not copy its wording so as not to be lengthy.

And in Sefer Ta'amei HaMitzvot of the sage Rabbi Yitzchak ben Farchiya, peace be upon him, he explained, concerning the severity of the oath, in the commandment "you shall not take," in these words: "you shall not take the Name of the LORD your God in vain" - for one who swears falsely cuts and separates the bridegroom from the bride - and this is "lo tissa" [you shall not lift/take], meaning: do not raise and elevate the LORD away from your God. And because one who swears falsely blemishes this seventh attribute [Malchut], therefore his punishment is so severe, "and shall consume its timber and its stones." And therefore it is juxtaposed with (Exodus 20:8), "remember the Sabbath day to sanctify it" - for the Sabbath is the male, and one must sanctify it and not separate it, Heaven forfend. He further wrote, that one who swears is as though he takes hold of the precious object of the supernal covenant in his hand, and the proof is (Genesis 24:2), "put now your hand under my thigh" - and if, Heaven forfend, he swears in vain and falsely, he cuts and separates.

Further, I heard in the name of the Kabbalists that in the verse "you shall not take" there are seventeen words, corresponding to the numerical value of "tov" [good], and to the numerical value of YHVH spelled out in full, and to the numerical value of "Torah," and to the numerical value of "seven" - to allude that one who swears falsely is uprooted from the good of the World to Come and from the rest mentioned, and from the sevenfold aspects alluded to in the oath [shevuah, related to sheva, seven] - for "shevuah" written defectively and vocalized totals sixty-six, the numerical value of Adonai plus the inclusive count.

And included in the matter of the oath is being careful not to mention the Name of Heaven in vain, for whoever mentions it in vain is liable to excommunication (Nedarim 7b), and this is included in "you shall not take," as explained. And whoever is careful about this has a great reward in the World to Come, as it is written (Malachi 3:20), "but for you who fear My Name, the sun of righteousness shall rise" - and they explained in Nedarim (8b), these are people who fear to bring forth the Name of Heaven in vain - to this point. And the explanation of "the sun of righteousness" is explained in the Gate of Fear, chapter 13.

Also included in oaths is that one not extend his hand to his beard and swear, for this is [equivalent to] an oath - and so explained in the Idra of Naso (end of page 131a), in these words: and whoever extends his hand to his beard to swear is as one who swears by the thirteen adornments of the beard - to this point. Also, one should be careful not to swear "by truth," for YHVH is called "truth," as it is said (Jeremiah 10:10), "and the LORD, God, is truth." And likewise one should be careful not to swear "by my life," for the soul is a portion of God from above, and is found to be like swearing by the Name.

Further, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 416, and siman 991) that one should not say "so may I merit the life of the World to Come" unless it is truly so. Further it is written there (siman 420) that in this era one should not swear to fulfill the commandments, for Satan will accuse and he will not fulfill his oath - and there is support for this from the teaching of Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Parashat Matot), which we copied above, saying (Deuteronomy 10:20), "you shall fear the LORD your God, Him you shall serve," and so on - if you have all these qualities, you may swear.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:14-: And concerning the sin of vows, they said in Tractate Nedarim (20a): it was taught, a person should never be accustomed to vows, for he shall eventually come to betray oaths. Further we read there (22a): the grandson of Rabbi Yannai the elder came before Rabbi Yannai the Great. He said to him, had you known that your record is opened and your deeds examined, would you have made a vow? And further he said, what did Rabban Gamliel open with, to that elder? "There is one who speaks rashly, like the piercings of a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing" (Proverbs 12:18). Further there: whoever speaks rashly deserves to be pierced with a sword, but the tongue of the wise is healing. Further there: it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, whoever vows is as though he built a high place [an illicit altar], and whoever fulfills it is as though he offered a sacrifice on it, and so on - and one who fulfills it without having his vow annulled [when he could] is as though he offered on that high place and is liable for slaughtering outside [the Temple].

Further there, Shmuel said, whoever vows, even though he fulfills it, is called wicked. Rabbi Abahu said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall not be a sin in you" (Deuteronomy 23:23) - and he derives "cheder" from "cheder" [same root, "cease/refrain"]: it is written here, "but if you refrain from vowing," and it is written there (Job 3:17), "there the wicked cease [chadlu] from raging" - to this point.

And in chapter 10 (Nedarim 77b) we read: Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, taught, whoever vows, even though he fulfills it, is called a sinner. Rav Zevid said, what is the verse? "But if you refrain from vowing, it shall not be a sin in you" - implying that if you do not refrain, there is a sin - to this point.

Further there, they said in Tractate Shabbat (32b): it was taught, Rabbi Natan says, because of the sin of vows, a man's wife dies, as it is said (Proverbs 22:27), "if you have nothing with which to pay, why should he take your bed from under you." Rabbi says, because of the sin of vows, children die while young, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 5:5), "do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin, and do not say before the angel that it was an error; why should God be angry at your voice, and destroy the work of your hands" - and "the work of a person's hands" refers to his sons and daughters - to this point, relevant here. And the reason for this is because vows are in the supernal Mother, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna, and one must fulfill his vow and bring it to the place of action, which is the Shechinah - and if, Heaven forfend, he did not fulfill it, the sin is in the children and in the lower Mother, and therefore his wife dies.

And in Midrash Kohelet (Rabbah 5:3) they explained this verse concerning those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. And incidentally we shall copy the severity of the sin of vows explained earlier there (Kohelet Rabbah 5:2), on the verse "it is better that you not vow," in these words: Rav Huna said, there was a story of one who vowed and did not pay, and set sail on the great sea, and his ship sank at sea and he died. Rabbi Shmuel said, whoever vows and does not pay causes his own wife to die, as it is written (Genesis 48:7), "and as for me, when I came from Padan, Rachel died to me [alai]" - and so it is explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayishlach, page 175a), that Jacob was punished for a vow he did not fulfill, and this troubled Jacob more than all the distresses that passed over him - and from where do we know that it was because of Jacob? Because it is written "Rachel died to me [alai]" - "alai" certainly, because I delayed my vow - to this point.

Further there, in the Midrash, Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever vows and does not pay causes himself to come to transgression - idolatry, forbidden relations, and bloodshed - and all are learned from Jacob: idolatry, as it is written (Genesis 35:2), "put away the foreign gods that are among you"; forbidden relations, as it is written, "for he had defiled Dinah their sister"; bloodshed, as it is written (ibid. 35:25), "and the two sons of Jacob took," and so on; and slander, as it is written (ibid. 31:1), "and he heard the words of Laban's sons." Rabbi Mana said, whoever vows and does not pay causes death to himself, as it is said (Deuteronomy 23:22), "for the LORD your God will surely require it of you." And Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity - there is no death without sin, as it is said (Ezekiel 18:20), "the soul that sins, it shall die" - and no suffering without iniquity, as it is said (Psalms 89:33), "then I will visit their transgression with the rod, and their iniquity with plagues."

"Do not let your mouth cause your flesh to sin" - Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse as referring to those who pledge charity publicly and do not give. "And do not say before the angel" - this is the cantor - "that it was an error" - let it be [regarded as] mine; "why should God be angry at your voice" - at that voice you spoke [in pledging]; "and destroy the work of your hands" - the diminishing of the commandments in that man's hand, the Holy One, blessed be He, brings a curse into them and destroys them from him - to this point.

And in the Midrash (Vayikra Rabbah, Parashat Arachin) this teaching of Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani is brought, that whoever vows and delays his vow eventually comes to idolatry, forbidden relations, bloodshed, and slander, and he proves all this from Jacob as stated in the teaching. However, it says there, Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said, whoever vows and pays has a reward for the vowing and for the paying, as it is said (Psalms 76:12), "vow and pay to the LORD your God" - and whoever vows and delays his vow causes death to himself, as it is written (Deuteronomy 23:22), "for the LORD your God will surely require it of you" - from you, punishment is exacted, and not from your money. Rabbi Ami said, there is no death without sin - to this point, relevant here.

And it appears to me that the end of the verse, "and there shall be a sin in you," shall be understood along the lines explained in the Zohar (Parashat Acharei Mot, page 75b), "that He see no unseemly thing among you" (Deuteronomy 23:15), explained above (chapter 11), that the intent is that that sin is imprinted literally in his body - along these lines, "shall require it," which they explained, of blessed memory, as death, because speech makes a real happening within his very body, that the sin is marked upon him - and this is "and there shall be [vehayah] in you" - the sin itself in your very being - and therefore punishment is exacted from you.

And without doubt, what it says, that one who vows and pays has a reward for the vow and for the payment, refers to vows of commandments, or consecration, or Torah - and Scripture is precise about this, saying "to the LORD your God" - and further Scripture says "all around Him" [in the context of the fear surrounding Him] - for the vow or the oath is given only to one who fears Heaven, who is around the Holy One, blessed be He, along the lines of (Psalms 50:3), "and it is very tempestuous around Him" - which our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained (Yevamot 121b), teaching that the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to a hairsbreadth - and so it is proven from the teaching we copied above from Midrash Rabbah (Parashat Matot).

Further, we read in Midrash Eichah (Rabbati 2:14), on the verse (Lamentations 2:10), "they sit on the ground" - Rabbi Elazar said, do not let the portion of vows be light in your eyes, for through the portion of vows the Great Sanhedrin of Zedekiah were killed, and so on - and the rest of the story, see there, so as not to be lengthy - and this same story is also brought in Nedarim (65a), with a slight difference between them.

And Rabbeinu Yaakov wrote (Yoreh De'ah, siman 203) that if they are pledging charity publicly and one must pledge with them, he should say "without a vow" - however, if it is a commandment incumbent on himself and obligatory upon him, such as one who says, I shall study this chapter, I shall study this tractate, and he fears lest he grow lax in the matter, though he has the ability to fulfill it, it is permitted for the vower to vow, to strengthen himself - for Rav Gidal said, from where do we know that one may swear to fulfill a commandment? As it is said (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn, and I will fulfill it, to observe Your righteous judgments." And all the more so where he is accustomed to forgetting and transgressing one of the negative commandments, or is lax in fulfilling a positive commandment, it is permitted for him to vow and swear, to be strict with himself to keep and fulfill the commandments - and concerning this our Sages, of blessed memory, said (Avot, chapter 3, mishnah 13), "vows are a fence for abstinence." But from all other vows a person must distance himself greatly - to this point. And we have already written above that it is not fitting to swear and vow even to fulfill a commandment, unless the person is God-fearing enough that he will fulfill his vow.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:26-: And in Midrash Bereshit Rabbah, on the verse (Genesis 28:20), "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying," they explained that it is permitted, and even good, to vow in a time of distress, to perform a commandment and the like, in these words: "and Jacob vowed a vow, saying" - it is written (Psalms 66:14), "which my lips uttered, and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress" - Rabbi Yitzchak the Babylonian said, "and my mouth spoke, when I was in distress" - that he vowed a commandment at the time of his distress. What is "saying"? For [future] generations, so that they vow at the time of their distress. Jacob opened with a vow first, therefore whoever vows should attach the vow only to Him. Rabbi Abahu said, it is written (Psalms 132:2), "who swore to the LORD, vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob" - "to the Mighty One of Abraham" or "to the Mighty One of Isaac" is not written here, but "to the Mighty One of Jacob" - he attached the vow to the one who opened with it first - to this point. And nevertheless, it is written in Sefer Chasidim (siman 403), that one who is in distress should not vow, but rather think and take counsel before there is a matter he can fulfill.

And know that whoever vows to fulfill a commandment or to occupy himself with Torah for so many hours a day and the like, it is not fitting to have his vow annulled unless he shows the court that it is a great compulsion - and if they annul it for him and there was no great compulsion in the matter, Heaven does not annul it for him - and this is what they were precise about, of blessed memory, in saying (Nedarim 8a), "a great vow he vowed to the God of Israel" - that the Holy One, blessed be He, should say, what wrong did you find in Me, that you have distanced yourself from Me? And it is like the parable of a man who says to a king of flesh and blood, by your head, my lord, on such-and-such a day I shall bring you such-and-such a gift - that if he does not bring it, his head becomes forfeit to the king, unless the king knows he was prevented by circumstances beyond his control. And the matter of occupying oneself with Torah or a commandment is literally a gift to the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, and whoever is lenient and annuls his vow is lenient with the honor of the King of the universe. And this is unlike annulling one's own personal vows, such as that he will or will not eat [something], where it is a commandment that he have his vow annulled, since there is no commandment involved in the matter.

And I heard from my teacher, peace be upon him, also a fitting matter concerning vows - he said that one who vows to perform a commandment, behold, at his utterance one angel is created, but its formation is not completed until the fulfillment of the commandment is complete - for it is known (cf. Avot, chapter 4, mishnah 11) that one who performs one commandment acquires for himself one advocate - and one who vows and does not pay his vow, that angel is found hanging and standing, and it is a distress to him until that act of the commandment is completed.

And whoever wishes his prayer to be heard and his request granted should strive to complete his vows, as it is written (Psalms 50:14), "offer to God thanksgiving, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon Me in the day of trouble, I will deliver you, and you shall glorify Me" - and so it is written in the Book of Job (22:27), "you shall make your prayer to Him, and He shall hear you, and you shall pay your vows... you shall decree a thing, and it shall be established for you." And these vows are certainly vows to Heaven that it is a commandment to fulfill - and this is its saying "and pay your vows to the Most High" - for concerning permitted matters, which are below, worldly matters, the phrase "your vows to the Most High" would not be accurate. Now, measure for measure - for in prayer he asks in speech that the Holy One, blessed be He, do such-and-such for him - He says to him, you fulfill in deed what you vowed, and I too shall do and fulfill the request of your mouth that depends on speech. And it is already known what they said in the Zohar several times (Parashat Lech Lecha, page 77b), "an arousal below, an arousal above" - that one must always precede with an arousal below.

And concerning "vows are a fence for abstinence," it is fitting for a wise person not to vow things that need to be annulled, but rather to vow for one day or half a day - as we find (Makkot 24a) Rabbi Yochanan, who would say, I am in a fast until I come home - and this is (Psalms 15:4), "who swears to his own hurt, and does not change." And even for a fast of [certain] hours, so that he can recite the "Aneinu" prayer, it is like this: he accepts upon himself, while it is still day, a fast until a certain hour of the day, and afterward decides to complete the day in a fast, reciting "Aneinu." And this is a good method for one who is weak, that he accept a fast upon himself and not need to have his vow annulled the next day - and when he completes that day in holiness, he accepts upon himself another day like the previous one, and it is found that all his days are in repentance. But he should not accept to make such-and-such a number of consecutive fasts, for immediately his inclination will stand against him with all its ability to nullify him from his service - and if a person does his matters discreetly and deals with his inclination cunningly, like Jacob's dealing with Esau, he can take away its blessing. And along these lines it is possible that the poet intended in saying in the psalm (Psalms 61:9), "so I will sing praise to Your Name forever, that I may daily perform my vows."

However, so as not to forget to accept his vow for another day, it is good that he seek a companion to encourage him, or make a booklet and write his acceptance there, and keep it with him always, so that he remember his matter. And this way is fitting for every person of action, for just as a merchant makes a book to reckon his expenses, so it is fitting that a penitent make a book to reckon his days, whether he spent them properly or not - and through this he fulfills (Psalms 51:5), "and my sin is ever before me."

Further, of this kind of discourse, one must be careful of excommunications and bans - and concerning the punishment of a ban, they elaborate in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer (chapter 37): know the power of a ban - come and see from the tribes, who were zealous concerning the licentiousness of the tribe of Benjamin - the Holy One, blessed be He, said to them, you were zealous concerning the licentiousness but not zealous concerning the idol of Micah - and because they were not zealous concerning the idol of Micah, therefore the children of Benjamin killed among them a first, second, and third time, until they fell before the Ark of the Covenant of the LORD and sought to repent, and the Holy One, blessed be He, was appeased toward them, and they placed a ban that all Israel go with them from great to small, as it is said (Judges 21:5), "for the great oath was" - but did all Israel swear an oath? Rather, this teaches you that the ban is the oath - and the men of Jabesh-Gilead were not with them in the assembly and were liable to death, as it is said, "whoever came not up to the LORD at Mizpah shall surely be put to death" - to this point.

Further there in Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Akiva says, the ban is the oath and the oath is the ban, and whoever breaks the oath is as though he broke the ban, and whoever breaks the ban breaks the oath - and whoever knows a matter and does not tell it, the ban comes upon him and consumes him and his timber and his stones, as it is said (Zechariah 5:4), "and I have sent it forth, says the LORD, and it shall come into the house of the thief, and into the house of him who swears falsely by My Name, and it shall lodge inside his house, and shall consume it, its timber and its stones." Know the power of the ban - come and see from Joshua son of Nun, who placed Jericho under a ban - to this point.

Further, one must be careful not to say, "let me be excommunicated if I do not do such-and-such," for even if he fulfills the condition, annulment is needed - and so our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained in Tractate Makkot (11b): Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav, an excommunication, even conditional, requires release - from where do we know this? From Judah, as it is written (Genesis 43:9), "if I do not bring him to you and set him before you, then let me bear the blame forever" - and it is written (Deuteronomy 33:6), "let Reuben live and not die," and then, "and this for Judah" - all those forty years Israel were in the wilderness, Judah's bones were rolled about in the coffin, until Moses stood and sought mercy for him, saying before Him, Master of the universe, who caused Reuben to confess [his sin]? Judah [who confessed first, as a model] - immediately, "hear, O LORD, the voice of Judah" - to this point, relevant here.

Further, one must be careful not to pronounce the Name by its letters, as we read in the first chapter of Avodah Zarah (17b): they brought Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon [before the Romans]. They said to him, why do you occupy yourself with Torah? He said to them, as the LORD my God commanded me. They immediately decreed that he be burned, his wife killed, and his daughter made to sit in a brothel. Him, to be burned, because he would pronounce the Name by its letters - but how could he do this, when we have learned (Sanhedrin, chapter 10, mishnah 1), and these have no share in the World to Come: one who says the Torah is not from Heaven, and that resurrection of the dead is not from the Torah; Abba Shaul says, also one who pronounces the Name by its letters! [Answer:] he did it in order to learn, as it was taught, "you shall not learn to do" [the practices of the nations] but you may learn to understand and to instruct [others] - so why was he punished? Because he pronounced the Name publicly. His wife, to be killed, because she did not protest against him - from here they said, whoever has the ability to protest and does not protest is punished for it - to this point.

And the Tosafot wrote (page 18a, s.v. "hogeh"): "pronounces the Name" - one explanation is that he expounds it through the forty-two-letter Name and does with it whatever he wishes; but most explain that he would pronounce explicitly the letters of the Explicit Name, like the letters of other words - and this is not fitting to do, as we say in Pesachim (50a), "not as I am written am I called - I am written with Yud-Heh and called with Alef-Dalet" - and it appears to Rabbi Yitzchak that one should not even mention the letters Yud-Heh as people are accustomed to do, since Yud-Heh is [part of] the Explicit Name - to this point.

"To learn" [it is permitted] to do, as was taught, and so on - and Rashi, of blessed memory, explained. However, the Holy One, blessed be He, is exacting with the righteous to a hairsbreadth, and even for the sake of learning, there is regard for the teacher's honor - and the verse "you shall not learn to do" they established as referring to other matters, such as the planting of cucumbers in Sanhedrin (68a), and the likeness of moon-shapes of Rabban Gamliel (Rosh Hashanah 24a). And the Tosafot wrote, and it appears that his text did not have "rather, why was he punished - was it that he pronounced it publicly?" and therefore he needed to give another reason - to this point.

Further, one must be careful not to speak slander against Israel, and so it says in the Yalkut (Melachim, siman 218, page 33, col. 3): why are Israel likened to a nut? As it is said, "I went down to the garden of nuts" (Song of Songs 6:11) - just as this nut is smooth, and whoever is not skilled at climbing it immediately falls - one must guard himself from falling from it - so whoever serves Israel must guard himself from taking what belongs to him from under their hand. Moses said (Numbers 20:10), "hear now, you rebels," and it was said to him (ibid. 20:12), "therefore you shall not bring this congregation." Isaiah said (Isaiah 6:5), "and I dwell among a people of unclean lips" - immediately (6:6), "and in his hand a glowing coal [ritzpah]" - what is "ritzpah"? Rabbi Shimon bar Nachmani said, it crushed [ratzatz] the mouth [peh], for he spoke slander against My children. Elijah said (1 Kings 19:10), "for the children of Israel have forsaken Your covenant" - and what was said to him? (19:16), "and Elisha son of Shafat you shall anoint as prophet in your place."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:39-: Rabbi Yochanan derived this from this verse (Isaiah 17:1-2), "the burden of Damascus," and so on, "standing in Damascus and proclaiming the cities of Aroer" - but is Aroer not only in the territory of Moab? Rather, there were three hundred sixty-five houses of idols in Damascus, and they would worship each one on its own day, and they had one day when they would worship them all - that same night, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, Elijah, before you accuse My children, go on your way to Damascus and accuse them.

Rabbi Abahu and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish were going up to Caesarea. Rabbi Abahu said to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, why are we going up to their city, which blasphemes and curses? Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish got down from his donkey, took some sand, and put it in his mouth. He said to him, what is this? He said to him, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not desire one who speaks slander against Israel, as it is written (Song of Songs 1:6), "do not look at me, that I am swarthy," and it is written (Proverbs 30:10), "do not slander a servant to his master" - to this point.

And there in the Yalkut (Melachim, siman 217, page 33, col. 3), before this, on the verse (1 Kings 19:19 - actually 19:9), "what are you doing here, Elijah?" - it was taught in the school of Elijah: he should have said before Him, Master of the universe, behold, Your children are the children of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who did Your will in Your world - but he did not do so, and instead said, "I have been very zealous," and so on. The Holy One, blessed be He, began to speak words of consolation to him, saying, when I descended to give the Torah, Israel did not descend with Me, only the ministering angels, who desired their good, as it is said (1 Kings 19:11), "go out and stand on the mountain," and so on, "and after the earthquake, fire" - He waited for him three hours, and he still stood by his first words and said, "I have been very zealous." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, "and Elisha son of Shafat you shall anoint as prophet in your place" - what you intend, he too can do. He said to Him, forever You are zealous, and so on - to this point.

And it is good for a person to train his tongue to teach in defense of Israel, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Yelamdenu concerning Gideon, who said (Judges 6:13), "and where are all His wonders?" - in these words: Rabbi Yehudah bar Shalom said, that night was the night of Passover, that he said to him, "and where are all His wonders?" Where are the wonders God did for our forefathers on this night, and struck all the firstborn of Egypt and brought Israel out from there rejoicing? And since he taught in defense of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, it is fitting that I reveal Myself in My glory to him, as it is said (ibid. 6:14), "and the LORD turned to him and said, go in this your strength." The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, you have the strength to teach in defense of Israel - by your merit they shall be redeemed, as it is said, "and save Israel" - to this point.

And further we read in Sanhedrin: Rabbi Acha said, we find that whoever teaches in defense of Israel, the Holy One, blessed be He, exalts him in the world, as it is written (Isaiah 30:18), "and therefore the LORD shall wait, to be gracious to you, and therefore He shall be exalted, to have mercy on you" - from whom do you learn this? From Achimaatz son of Zadok, as it is said (2 Samuel 18:19), "and Achimaatz son of Zadok said, let me run and bring the king news," and, "and he said, is it well with the young man, with Absalom?" And Achimaatz said, "I saw a great tumult," and, "and the king said, turn aside and stand here, and he turned aside and stood" (18:29-30). Rabbi Abba bar Kahana said, had he been a duke, he would have become a governor; had he been a governor, a commander [for his loyal but incomplete report]. "And behold, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, let my lord the king receive good tidings," and so on, "and the king said to the Cushite, is it well with the young man, with Absalom?" And the Cushite said, "may the enemies of my lord the king... be as that young man," and so on, "and the king was troubled, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept" (18:31-33, 19:1)] - what is "and the king was troubled"? Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina said, this alludes to his blows [i.e., the Cushite was made to suffer for his blunt bad news]. Now is this not an a fortiori argument - if Achimaatz, who said neither good nor bad about the king's son, merited all this honor, one who teaches in defense of the children of the Omnipresent, all the more so - to this point.

And so in Vayikra Rabbah (Parashah 10:1), "take Aaron," on the verse (Psalms 45:8), "you love righteousness and hate wickedness" - this verse is explained concerning Abraham, who sought merit for the people of Sodom, as explained there. The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him, you loved to justify My creatures and not to condemn them - "therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows" - what is "above your fellows"? He said to him, by your life, of the ten generations from Noah to you, I did not speak with any one of them, but with you I speak, as it is said (Genesis 15:1), "after these things."

Further, this verse is explained there concerning Isaiah - the Holy One, blessed be He, said, Isaiah My son, they are troublesome, they are rebellious - if you accept upon yourself to be disgraced and struck by My children, you may go on My mission, and if not, you shall not go on My mission. He said to Him, on this condition: "I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to those who plucked out the hair" (Isaiah 50:6), and I am not worthy to go on a mission to Your children. The Holy One, blessed be He, said, Isaiah, "you love righteousness" - you loved to justify My children - "and hate wickedness" - you hated to condemn them - "therefore God, your God, has anointed you" - what is "above your fellows"? He said to him, by your life, all the other prophets received prophecy, prophet from prophet, "and He drew from the spirit that was upon him," and so on (Numbers 11:25), "and they said, the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha" (2 Kings 2:15) - but you, from the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is said (Isaiah 61:1), "the spirit of the LORD God is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me," and so on. By your life, all the prophets [prophesied] simple prophecies, but you, doubled consolations - "awake, awake" (ibid. 51:9), "arouse yourself, arouse yourself" (ibid. 51:17), "I will greatly rejoice" (ibid. 61:10), "I, I am He who comforts you" (ibid. 51:12), "comfort, comfort" (ibid. 40:1) - to this point.

Further, one must be careful not to engage in idle talk in the synagogue - and so Rabbeinu Yaakov wrote (Orach Chaim, siman 151): synagogues and study halls should not be treated with levity, such as jesting, mockery, and idle talk. And in the Zohar (Parashat Terumah, page 131b): whoever converses in the synagogue, woe to him, for he shows separation; woe to him, for he diminishes faith; woe to him, for he has no portion in the God of Israel, for he shows that there is no God and He is not found there, and he has no portion in Him, and does not fear Him, and conducts himself disgracefully toward the supernal repair above - to this point.

And although at first glance, from the wording, it appears that all these severities are stated only concerning the time of prayer - as it says right afterward, that at the time Israel arrange in the synagogue the order of songs and praises and the order of prayer, three camps of supernal angels gather - nevertheless, since the synagogue is a holy place, the dwelling of the Shechinah, our Rabbis, of blessed memory, forbade thinking about calculations there at any time, unless they are calculations for a commandment (Tur, ibid.; cf. Megillah 28b) - certainly one should not converse in ordinary or idle talk, which is forbidden even outside the synagogue, as it is written (Deuteronomy 6:7), "and you shall speak of them" - and not of idle matters - from here, one who converses in ordinary or idle talk transgresses a positive commandment (cf. Yoma 19b).

The general rule that emerges is that wherever there is holiness, one must conduct oneself with awe, as it is written (Genesis 28:17), "how awesome is this place; this is none other than the house of God." And in the precepts of Rashbi, peace be upon him (Zohar, Parashat Beshalach, page 59b), it says that the lower synagogue stands corresponding to the supernal synagogue - and when a person pictures this matter in his mind, he shall fear and be afraid and pray with intent, for the supernal synagogue is called a fire of brightness, and the souls of the righteous enter it only to pray, not to converse about idle matters - and correspondingly the synagogue is called a fire of brightness, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Ki Teitzei, page 282a), and therefore they call the synagogue "esh nogah" [fire of brightness].

And it is written in Sefer HaRokeach (Laws of Repentance): one who speaks in the synagogue while his companions praise and sing, I apply to him (Jeremiah 12:14), "concerning all my evil neighbors" - "for the ways of the LORD are right, and the just walk in them, but transgressors stumble in them" (Hosea 14:10) - and one who does not join his companions and disdains praising his Maker encroaches on the Creator's territory - "and I will be to them a small sanctuary" (Ezekiel 11:16) - these are the synagogues, in which levity should not be practiced, as we say in chapter 3 of Megillah (28b-29a) - "God stands in the congregation of God" (Psalms 82:1), and one who speaks acts as though he turns his back to Him - He shall say, why did I come and there was no man, I called and none answered (cf. Isaiah 50:2), I stretched out My hand and none paid heed (Proverbs 1:24) - why should the LORD be angry at your voice and say to you, who has required this of your hand, to trample My courts (cf. Isaiah 1:12)? Rather, bow to Him and turn before Him in awe, with a bowed head, in humility, with the treasures of the heart supplicate before Him, and sing before Him with joy, and come before Him with jubilation - then He shall be near to you and found by you, and you shall unify the Name of Heaven with intent of heart, and pray with intent of heart - and when you say "Blessed are You," if you think of idle matters it is as though you mocked Him, not placing His fear upon your face - rather, think that He stands facing you, "I have set the LORD before me always" (Psalms 16:8), and place His fear upon your face and His love within you, and direct your whole heart, and be modest before Him, and confess your sins and seek Him, and He shall be found by you, and you shall bless Him - to this point.

And if it is not possible for everyone, at least Torah scholars who fear sin should take this matter to heart, and not begin to speak with each other in the synagogue about their business, even not at the time of prayer, so that they conduct themselves with awe in the synagogue - and if someone who has not conducted himself thus speaks to them, they should answer him briefly.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Holiness 14:51-: And so was the custom of my teacher, peace be upon him, not to speak within the sukkah on the days of the Sukkot festival except in words of Torah, for the holiness of the commandment of the sukkah is great, and the proof is that the wood of the sukkah has holiness attached to it and is forbidden [to use for other purposes] the whole seven days, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sukkah 9a).

And so we find that Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained (Zohar, Parashat Emor, end of page 103) that the Patriarchs come to the sukkah, and said: like Rav Hamnuna Sabba, who, when he entered the sukkah, would rejoice and stand at the entrance of the sukkah from within, and say, let us invite the guests. He would arrange the table and stand on his feet and bless, and say, "in sukkot you shall dwell" - sit, supernal guests, sit, sit, guests of faith, sit. He would raise his hands and rejoice and say, happy is our portion, happy is the portion of Israel, as it is written (Genesis 32:9), "for the LORD's portion is His people" - and he would sit - to this point. And above this, the previous column, he called the sukkah "the shade of faith," and said, whoever sits beneath the shade of faith inherits freedom for himself and his children forever, and is blessed with a supernal blessing, and so on.

Behold, a person within the sukkah is surrounded by an air of holiness, and how many holinesses are in it, as explained - and therefore it is fitting to distance oneself from conversation and jesting, but rather fulfill "and rejoice with trembling" - for the place alluded to by the sukkah is joy and trembling, from which judgments are aroused (Zohar, Parashat Acharei Mot, page 65a), and the days of Sukkot are judgment - and the proof is that on the night of Hoshana Rabbah is the sealing of judgment, and these days must be spent in repentance and trembling, for these days are given in order to extend the time for a person to repent, and the notes of the decrees are not handed over to the messengers until the night of the eighth day, Shemini Atzeret, as explained in the Zohar (Parashat Vayechi, page 220a), in these words: come and see, when judgment is aroused in the world, when the Holy One, blessed be He, sits on the throne of judgment, a person must arouse repentance in judgment, to turn from liability - for on that day the notes are written and all found in wrath are written - whichever person repents before his Master, the notes concerning him are torn up; afterward the Holy One, blessed be He, appoints a time before a person, the Day of Atonement, the day of repentance - if he repents from his sins, he repents, and if not, the King commands that the notes be sealed, woe, for repentance must depart from him; if he merits complete, proper repentance, they hang suspended over him until that final day of Atzeret, which is the eighth day, and if he makes complete repentance before his Master, they are torn up; and if he does not merit it, those notes go out from the King's house and are delivered into hand, and judgment is executed, and the notes never return again to the King's house - then the images depart - to this point, relevant here.

Further, one must be careful not to converse in ordinary talk on the Sabbath, and so it is explained in Midrash Tanchuma (beginning of Parashat Bereshit), on the verse (Isaiah 58:13), "and honor it, not doing your own ways, nor finding your own pleasure, nor speaking your own words," in these words: "nor speaking your own words" - like the mother of Rashbi, who, when she was talking on the Sabbath, he said to her, it is the Sabbath day, and be silent. Rabbi Yochanan said, out of necessity they permitted greeting people on the Sabbath - to this point. And so the Tosafot copied this midrash (s.v. "shelo yehei") in the chapter "Elu Kesharim" (Shabbat 113b).

And further they said in the Midrash (cf. Pesikta Rabbati, chapter 23): just as He rested from speaking, so you shall rest from speaking - for by the word of the LORD the heavens were made (Psalms 33:6), and His work was speech, and what is said of Him (Genesis 2:2), "and He rested on the seventh day," is a resting from speech - so too a person, likewise.

And in the Zohar (Parashat Vayakhel, page 205b), in these words: when Israel enter the synagogue, it is forbidden to occupy oneself even with the needs of the synagogue, but only with matters of praise, prayer, and Torah as is fitting for them - and whoever occupies himself with other matters, worldly matters, on this day, is a person who profanes the Sabbath, and has no portion among the people of Israel. Two angels are appointed over this on the Sabbath day, and they place their hands on his head and say, woe to so-and-so, who has no portion in the Holy One, blessed be He. And therefore one must occupy himself with prayer and with songs and praises of his Master, and occupy himself with Torah - this day is the day of souls, when that bundle of souls is crowned with the praises of their Master - therefore they praise with the praise of the soul, and this is "the soul of every living thing shall bless Your Name, O LORD our God, and the spirit of all flesh" - and there is no praise except from the side of the soul and the spirit, and this day stands in spirit and soul, it is not [a day] of the body - to this point.

Now, for this reason we shall understand why our Rabbis, of blessed memory, forbade (Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat, chapter 15, halachah 3) asking for one's needs on the Sabbath - that one prays on the Sabbath only seven blessings - because the day is a day of the soul and not a day of the body, and therefore one does not ask for the needs of the body. And from here the discerning reader shall judge to be strict with himself concerning ordinary talk - for if requesting for one's body is forbidden, all the more so is ordinary talk.

Further, one must be careful not to speak while the prayer leader repeats the Amidah, even words of Torah, but rather direct his intent to answer "amen" to each and every blessing, and his ears should be toward what the prayer leader utters from his mouth, and he should place his eyes below and his heart above, just as in his own silent prayer (Yevamot 105b) - and the reason, as explained in the Ra'aya Meheimna (Parashat Pinchas, page 229a), is that these are two unifications, and in the repetition of the Amidah it is a more excellent unification than the previous one, since he answers "amen" to each blessing, for "amen" totals the numerical value of the two Names "Yakdonki" [YHVH and Adonai combined] - which is not the unification when a person prays silently, for then he mentions the LORD by His appellation Adonai, and although his intent is toward YHVH, nevertheless the two Names are not interwoven as one - but in "amen" there is an allusion to the two Names being unified as one, so it is found to be a more excellent unification.

And this is the wording of Rashbi, peace be upon him, there, in brief: "greater is one who answers amen than one who blesses" - for [in the silent prayer] it is Adonai [facing] YHVH, and their faces and their wings, corresponding to the Name YHVH in the faces, corresponding to the Name Adonai in the wings, "one cherub from one end and one cherub from the other end" (Exodus 37:8) - but when the prayer leader repeats the prayer and one answers amen, it is in the second joining - "amen" - the two Names are joined in the second joining; at first [it was like] the loops corresponding to one another in the boards, which are the joints of the fingers, but with "amen" "and the Tabernacle shall be one" (Exodus 26:6), in which "the curtains shall be coupled together, one to another" - to this point.

Behold, it is explicit that the prayer leader's repetition of the prayer is a more excellent unification than the previous one, when he prayed silently - for the cherubim are "one cherub from one end," and so on - and if a person speaks during the prayer leader's repetition, he separates the unification, for there is no other speech there but "amen," which indicates the unification.

And so it is proven from here that when there is a repetition of the eighteen blessings by the prayer leader, one should not alter and say part of the prayer aloud, to say the Kedushah, and part silently - for such a prayer has no place, neither silent nor aloud, and nothing like this is found either in the Talmud or the Zohar.

And so it is also proven in Parashat Vayelech (Zohar, Parashat Vayelech, page 285b), that one must have an attentive ear to answer "amen" to every blessing - it says, on the verse (Isaiah 26:2), "who keeps faith [shomer emunim]" - meaning, guards that blessing which the blesser says, and waits to answer "amen" as needed - his soul ascends and proclaims before Him, "open the gates," and so on. And it says further there, we have learned, whoever hears from the blesser and does not intend "amen" concerning him, of him it is said (1 Samuel 2:30), "and those who despise Me shall be lightly esteemed" - as it says (Malachi 1:6), "you, O priests, who despise My Name" - and at the time it is needed, what is his punishment? Just as he did not open blessings above, so they do not open for him - and not only that, but when he departs from this world, they proclaim before him and say, shut the gates before so-and-so, let him not enter, do not receive him - woe to him, woe to his soul - to this point. And they elaborate further there on his punishment.
